newsitem.title: USA: IRS memo raises concerns but contracts valid - NGFA.
newsitem.headline: IRS memo raises concerns but contracts valid - NGFA.

text.p: Deferred-payment contracts for sale of grain remain a valid merchandising technique, a trade group attorney said Monday in the wake of concerns raised by an IRS technical advice memorandum.
"People shouldn't read more into it than it is," said David Barrett of the National Grain and Feed Association.
The Memo did not question the legality of deferred contracts.

Barrett and a spokeswoman for the Internal Revenue Service said the memos apply only to the set of facts and the taxpayer involved; in this case, how to consider income from deferred sales when calculating the alternative minimum tax.
"Yes, it (the memo) is a possible problem but it should not be blown out of proportion either," Barrett said.

The IRS has lost past cases when it argued that income from deferred-payment contracts on grain should be counted in the year the contract was entered even if the money exchanged hands later, he said.

At issue in the IRS memo was a farmer who sold potatos under an agreement that delayed part of the income until the next year although the sales price was determined on delivery. The IRS decided that all the income should be counted in the same tax year.
Deferred-payment contracts are a popular sales method for grain farmers, who often file income taxes on a calendar-year basis.

Farmers should consult with an accountant or tax adviser to determine if they need to calculate or pay the alternative miniumum tax, Barrett said. Even if they need to calculate the AMT, it may not result in any additional tax obligation.
